(p-٣٦٣٧)In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

**Surat al-Ra'd (The Thunder)**

It is named after the words of the Mighty and Majestic in it: ﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Ra'd: 13]. This indicates the negative and affirmative attributes, together with information about the unseen realities of the heavenly dominion (malakut), and because thunder combines warning and hope. These are among the greatest aims of the Qur'an, as said by al-Mahayimi.

The early scholars (al-Salaf, the earlier generations of Muslims) held two opinions on whether it is Meccan or Medinan. It is said that it is Medinan except for His words: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31] and the verse. It is also said that from its beginning to the end of ﴿And if there had been a Qur'an﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31] it is Medinan, and the rest of it is Meccan. And God knows best.

Its verses number forty-three.

(p-٣٦٣٨)In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[1] ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the verses of the Book. And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, but most of the people do not believe.﴾

Abu al-Su'ud said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra﴾ is a name of the surah. Its position may be in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this surah is named by this name. This is more apparent than its being in the nominative as a subject, since knowledge of the naming has not preceded. His words ﴿Those﴾ on the first reading is an independent subject. On the second reading it is a second subject, or an apposition to the first, indicated by it to signal its grandeur. It may also be in the accusative by supposing a verb that fits the context, such as "Recite" or "Mention." Then "Those" is a subject, as when ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra﴾ is taken as a listed sequence. The predicate, according to the various possibilities, is His words ﴿the verses of the Book﴾, meaning the wondrous Book, complete, free of any need to be described, known as such among books, deserving that the name "Book" be exclusively applied to it. It refers to the entire Qur'an, or to the whole of what was sent down at that time. His words ﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾, meaning from the Book mentioned in its entirety, ﴿is the truth﴾, meaning the established, which corresponds to reality in everything it states, deserving that truth be attributed to it because of its firmness in truth and the inferiority of anything else to its level of perfection. In expressing it by a relative pronoun, in attributing its sending down by the passive form of the verb, and in mentioning the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah) with its pronoun referring to him, peace be upon him, there is an indication of the grandeur of what was sent down, which accompanies the majesty of the one who sent it and the honor of the one to whom it was sent, and an allusion to the aspect of the predicate, which is not hidden. End of the summary with additions.

(p-٣٦٣٩)A subtle point (lata'if):

Regarding ﴿that which has been revealed﴾ there are two possibilities. The first is that it is in the nominative position, with ﴿the truth﴾ as its predicate; or the predicate is ﴿from your Lord﴾ and ﴿the truth﴾ is an omitted predicate, or a predicate following a predicate. The second is that its position is in the genitive by coordination with (the Book), coordination of the general with the specific, or one of the two attributes with the other; or by supposing an extra waw in the attribute, with (the truth) as an omitted predicate. Many grammarians prohibited the addition of waw in attributes. Others permitted it to emphasize joining, that is, gathering and connection, because just as it joins the conjoined noun with what it is conjoined to, so it joins the described noun with the attribute, and it indicates that his being described by it is a fixed matter. His words ﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾, meaning in that truth, because they reject reflecting upon it out of hostility and obstinacy. This is like His words: ﴿And most of the people will not believe, however eager you are﴾ [Yusuf: 103].

The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[2] ﴿It is Allah who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see. Then He rose over the Throne, and subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. He arranges the affair and details the signs, that you may be certain of meeting your Lord.﴾

He, the Exalted, informs of the perfection of His power and the greatness of His dominion: that it is He who, by His power, raised the heavens, meaning He created them elevated above the earth, at a height whose extent cannot be reached or comprehended. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿without pillars that you can see﴾ means without columns (ʾasāṭīn), the plural of ʿimād or ʿamūd. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿that you can see﴾ is either a resumed statement (istiʾnāf) serving as evidence by their seeing the heavens as such, like the saying of the poet:

"I am without sword or spear, yet you see me."

Or it is a qualifier of ʿamad (pillars), introduced to create ambiguity (ibhām), since they have pillars that are not visible. This is the view taken by many of the early generations (al-salaf). Ibn Kathir preferred the first reading, that there are no pillars, and said: "This is what is fitting to the context, and what is apparent from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ [al-Hajj: 65], and it is also more perfect in terms of power." His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Then He rose over the Throne﴾ has had its interpretation already given in the surah of al-Aʿraf, and that it is to be passed on as it came, without modality (takyif), without likening (tashbih), without negation (taʿtil), and without representation (tamthil).

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And subjected the sun and the moon﴾ means He made them submissive to what He willed from them of benefit to the lower world. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿each running for a specified term﴾ means for a determined end at which their course stops, which is the establishment of the Hour, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the sun runs toward its resting place﴾ [Ya-Sin: 38]. This is explained in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1] and ﴿When the stars fall, scattered﴾ [al-Infitar: 2]. The restriction to the sun and the moon is because they are the most apparent of the heavenly bodies and greater than others, so the subjection of others is by way of greater priority (bi-tariq al-awla). The subjection of both together with others has been stated explicitly in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command. Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 54].

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿He arranges the affair﴾ means: the affair of the upper and lower worlds; He directs it, governs it, and decrees it by His will and wisdom in the most perfect manner, and no matter occupies Him from another matter. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and details the signs﴾ means the signs that indicate His oneness, His power, and His sublime attributes; that is, He clarifies them in His revealed books. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿that you may be certain of meeting your Lord﴾ means: that you may be certain and believe that this Arranger and Detailer, there is no escape for you from returning to Him, through resurrection after death for recompense. For whoever reflects with true reflection will be certain that the One who is able to originate the aforementioned heavenly signs is able to restore and to recompense!

[p-3641] Subtleties (lataʾif):

The first: In His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Allah, who raised the heavens﴾, it is permissible that the relative pronoun (alladhi) be the predicate (khabar), and it is permissible that it be a qualifier (sifa), with the predicate being ﴿He arranges the affair﴾. In al-Kashshaf, the first is preferred, because His later saying ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾ [al-Raʿd: 3] is coordinated with it, in a contrast between the upper things and the lower things, and in the counterpart the predicative form is definite, so this too should be so for the two to be consistent. The sentence confirms His saying: ﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [al-Raʿd: 1]. He turned from the pronoun of the Lord to the Name of Majesty (al-Jalalah) to lend prominence to the confirmation, as if it were said: how could what was sent down not be the truth, from One whose acts are these? The definiteness of the two ends (the two terms) is to convey that He has no partner in them, especially since it is made a relative clause (silah) for the relative pronoun. This is more suited to the context than making it a qualifier that serves to establish that they are arranged and detailed, along with glorifying their matter. The intended benefit is His saying: ﴿that you may be certain of meeting your Lord﴾; the meaning being that He did all of it for that.

The second: Al-Qadi said: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿raised the heavens﴾ and so on is evidence of the existence of the Wise Creator, for their being raised above the other bodies that are equal to them in the essence of corporeality (jirmiyya), and their being specified with what requires that, must be due to a specifier that is neither a body nor corporeal, which prefers some possibilities over others by His will. Along this method is all the other signs mentioned.

The third: "yudabbiru" (He arranges) and "yufassilu" (He details) are read with the yaʾ and with the nun. Both are resumed statements (mustaʾnafan). Or the first is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "sakhkhara" (subjected), and the second from the pronoun in "yudabbiru", or both are from the pronouns of the mentioned verbs.

When he established the heavenly evidences, he followed them with mention of the lower indications of His power and wisdom. So He, the Exalted, said:

(p-3642) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[3] ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth and placed therein firmly set mountains and rivers, and of all the fruits He made therein two mates, two kinds, He covers the night with the day. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾

﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾, meaning He spread it out and made it wide and extended in length and breadth, so as to bring forth abundant blessings from it.

Al-Shihab said: Some have used this verse as evidence that the earth is flattened and is not in fact spherical. Whoever affirms its sphericity, they say, means only that flatness is the natural consequence of its nature. This is refuted by the fact that its sphericity has been established by rational proofs. However, because of the enormous size of its mass, every piece and region of it appears to the observer as if it were flat. The same is true of every great circle. No one knows its true shape except Him, exalted is He.

﴿And He placed therein firmly set mountains﴾, meaning mountains that are fixed, serving as stakes for it, in which vegetation abounds and beneath which water is preserved. ﴿And rivers﴾, gushing forth from them. This is for the multiplication of plants and trees and for the sustenance of animals. ﴿And of all the fruits He made therein two mates, two kinds﴾, meaning two categories, such as sweet and sour, black and white, small and large, and cultivated and wild.

Al-Mahayimi said: So that each kind may yield a benefit different from that of the other. Thus each kind is a blessing added to the bounty of the basic types, and it was made so as to complete the bounty through varieties of differing natures, lest they all combine and harm those who consume them, being of differing seasons, since:

﴿He covers the night with the day﴾, meaning He clothes the one in the place of the other, so that what was bright and luminous becomes black and dark. Through the lengthening of the night comes winter, through the lengthening of the day comes summer, through one of the two equinoxes comes autumn, and through the other comes spring. ﴿Indeed in that﴾, meaning in the spreading of the earth and what follows it, ﴿are signs for a people who reflect﴾. (p-3643) That is, they are manifest signs for a people who reflect, who thereby infer that the creation of what has been mentioned in this wondrous pattern necessarily requires a Powerful and Wise Creator. Or they reflect and come to know that the multiplication of blessings serves to attract the love of the Benefactor, by directing them to that for which they were created, and love necessarily leads to returning to Him. This also contains an indication that whoever arranged these things for their livelihood would surely bless them by sending messengers and revealing books that guide them to what brings them felicity. Indeed, and He is the Most Judicious of judges.

Subtleties:

First: Al-Razi said: Among the evidences drawn from the states of mountains is that rivers are generated on the surface of the earth because of them. This is because stone is a solid body. When vapours ascend from the depths of the earth and reach the mountain, they are held back there and continue to accumulate, so that vast waters form beneath the mountain. Then, because of their abundance and strength, they pierce through, emerge, and flow over the surface of the earth. The benefit of mountains in the generation of rivers is thus in this respect and for this reason. Therefore, in most cases wherever God mentions mountains, He joins with them the mention of rivers, as in this verse, and as in His saying: ﴿And We placed therein firmly set mountains, lofty, and gave you to drink sweet water﴾ [al-Mursalat: 27].

Second: Al-Razi pointed out that just as humankind began from a pair of two, the individual pair being Adam and Eve, so too plants and crops were first created from two pairs and then multiplied. And God knows best.

Third: In His saying ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾ there is a compound-figurative metaphor (istiʿarah tabʿiyyah tamthiliyyah), based on likening the removal of the light of the atmosphere to darkness, by covering apparent things with coverings. That is, He conceals the day with the night. Although the construction could also admit the reverse, by taking the second object as preceding the first, since the light of day likewise veils the darkness of night, it is more fitting that the night be the one that covers. This is counted among the lower signs within the verses, although its connection to the upper signs is evident, in that its manifestation is on the earth. (p-3644) For the night is only the shadow of the earth, and above the place of its shadow there is no night at all. Moreover, night and day are related to the fruits in terms of their setting and ripening, and they are also two opposites, paired like them.

It is also read as ﴿yughashshi﴾ from the verb of covering (taghshiyah), as Abu al-Su'ud has noted.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 13, verse 4:

Then Allah Most High explained a group of the signs by His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Most High:

[4] ﴿And in the earth are adjacent tracts, and gardens of grapevines, and crops, and palm trees, some multiple-trunked and some single-trunked, watered with one water; and We prefer some of them over others in fruit. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason.﴾

﴿And in the earth are adjacent tracts﴾ That is: adjacent plots of land, differing in their natures. Some are good, some are salt-marsh, some are hard, some are soft, which indicates a Capable, Arranging, Willing, Wise Maker in His craftsmanship.

﴿and gardens of grapevines, and crops, and palm trees, some multiple-trunked and some single-trunked﴾ "Sinwan" is the plural of "sinw," which is a palm whose root is one but whose branches are varied. In al-Qamus (the Lexicon): "The two palm trees, and whatever exceeds them, growing from one root, each one of them is a sinw, and it may be pronounced with a damma." Or it is general for all trees. The word "zar'" (crops) is in the singular because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar) that covers the few and the many.

﴿watered﴾ It is read with the yaa' (third person) and with the taa' (second person).

﴿with one water﴾ That is, with rainwater or with river water.

﴿and We prefer some of them over others in fruit﴾ So they differ in quantity, shape, scent and taste. "Ukul" (fruit) is read with a damma on the hamza and the kaf, and with the kaf sukun; it means what is eaten, and here it refers to fruit and grain. The prepositional phrase is either an adverb of time/place attached to "nufaddilu" (We prefer), or a circumstantial qualifier of "ba'duha" (some of them), meaning: We prefer some of them as edible. Or: in it is the eating.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ That is, what He has detailed.

﴿are signs﴾ of His Oneness and His dazzling power.

﴿for a people who reason﴾ For whoever reasons over what has preceded will be certain that the One who is able to originate and create them, varied in shapes, colours, tastes and scents, in those diverse adjacent plots, and made them gardens full of beauty, is able to restore what He originated; indeed, by analogy, that is even easier.

(p-3645)

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[5] ﴿And if you are astonished, then astonishing is their saying: "When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?" Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord. Those are the ones with shackles around their necks, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

﴿And if you are astonished, then astonishing is their saying: "When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ This is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). That is: if you are astonished at anything, then their saying is astonishing and truly deserves that wonder be confined to it. For whoever has witnessed the wondrous signs that have been enumerated, which point to a power before which every great thing becomes small, is certain that the One who is able to originate them and was not exhausted by creating them, re-creation is the easiest and simplest thing for Him. Thus their denial is one of the marvels of marvels. It is also permitted that the address be to everyone who is fit for it, meaning: if you are astonished, O you who have looked into these signs and known the power of the One whose acts these are, then increase in astonishment at those who, despite this, deny His power to resurrect, which is easier than these!

Abu al-Su'ud said: "The more suitable reading, given His saying ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6], is the first, and ('astonishing') is a predicate placed before its subject for restriction (al-qasr), and the emphasis is from the outset, by making their saying that a matter of wonder."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the deniers of His power to resurrect, ﴿are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord﴾, that is, they persisted in disbelief. For whoever denies the power of God, exalted is He, has indeed denied Him, because a god cannot be incapable. In this there is also a rejection of His report and that of His messengers, peace be upon them. ﴿And those have shackles around their necks﴾, that is, chains fastened to their necks, on their hands, on the Day of Resurrection, because they shackled their thoughts from reflecting on these matters, just as they made their Creator one whose power over that is shackled, while He is the All-Powerful, the All-Wise. ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

(p-3646) Discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[6] ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good, although exemplary punishments have already passed before them. And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment.﴾

﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾: that is, they ask you to hasten the punishment before the well-being and safety from it. This is because they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to bring them the punishment, mocking his warning.

Al-Shihab said: What is meant by it being "before the good" is that their asking for it precedes asking for it, or that their asking for it comes before the expiry of the time appointed for it!

﴿Although exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾: that is, punishments like theirs upon those who denied. So why do they not take heed from them, and why do they not fear the descent of the like of them? Or, the punishments that are cited as a proverb for severity. The clause is either circumstantial (ḥāliyyah) or resumptive (mustaʼnafah). "Al-mathulāt" is the reading of the majority, with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the tha', the plural of mathulah (like sumrah, plural sumarāt), meaning a disgracing punishment. It is so named because of the likeness between the punishment and what is punished for, as in His words: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. Or it is derived from mithal in the sense of retribution, as one says: amthaltuhu and aqsastuhu with one meaning. Or it is from the proverb (mathal) struck for its magnitude. It was also read with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the thaʼ (the dialect of the people of the Hijaz), and read with a damma on the mim and a sukun on the thaʼ, and read with both fatha and damma.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾. Some scholars took forgiveness in its common sense, which is the forgiveness of sins absolutely, except where evidence restricts it for those who do not profess tawhid, for their wrongdoing, meaning their shirk, is not forgiven. As for other than shirk, its forgiveness is subject to His will. Others held that forgiveness is intended in its linguistic meaning, which is covering and pardoning, by respite and delaying punishment until the Hereafter. That is: He is One of great forbearance who does not hasten punishment, even though they wrong and err (p-3647) by night and by day, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon the earth a single creature﴾ [Fatir: 45]. And this interpretation is more fitting to the awe-inspiring context!

It is strange of al-Shihab that he agreed with al-Razi in his claim that (delaying punishment is not called forgiveness, because it contradicts the apparent meaning and the usage of the Qur'an, and because it entails that all the disbelievers are forgiven on account of the postponement of their punishment until the Hereafter). Yet it is not hidden from you that calling it forgiveness is correct, since in language forgiveness is covering, and one of its instances is covering by respite. The claim that it contradicts the apparent meaning and the usage of the Qur'an is a sheer arbitrary imposition upon the style of the Qur'an, by reducing it to what they established. Moreover, appeal to it in matters of branches and roots is what is decisive, as it is the proof in language and usage! The claim that the entailment is corrupt and the magnitude of its consequence is exaggerated is baseless, since there is no objection to it, especially as it fits their hastening of the punishment mentioned earlier, so the implication is valid! Furthermore, it is established that the Qur'an explains one part of itself by another, so this verse in meaning is like the verse ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task﴾ [al-Nahl: 61], etc. Thus the interpretation mentioned is supported by this verse, so reflect, and do not be a captive of imitation!

When He, exalted is He, had made clear the breadth of His forbearance, He coupled it with the declaration of the severity of His punishment, so that hope and fear might be balanced. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾, that is, for whomever He wills, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they deny you, say: Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy, but His punishment will not be averted from the criminal people﴾ [al-An'am: 147]. He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-A'raf: 167]. And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-Hijr: 49] ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ [al-Hijr: 50].

(p-3648) On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[7] ﴿Those who disbelieve say: "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide.﴾

﴿Those who disbelieve say﴾: they are the ones who hasten on evil, the forerunners in disbelief.

Abu al-Su'ud said: He turned from the pronoun (idmar) to the relative construction (al-mawsul) in order to censure them and to denounce their disbelief in the signs of God, Exalted is He, before which the firm mountains would crumble. They paid no regard to them and did not count them among the kinds of signs. Out of obstinacy they said: ﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ That is, like the signs of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, or like what they proposed: turning the Safa into gold, or removing the mountains and putting in their place meadows and rivers. ﴿You are only a warner﴾: that is, you have been sent only to warn and frighten against the evil consequences of what they do and what they neglect, and to advise as other messengers did. Your duty is only to convey the message, not to grant the proposed demands. ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾: that is, a prophet who calls to the truth and guides by the sign that suits his time, as in His saying: ﴿And there has been no nation but a warner has passed among them﴾ (Fatir: 24). This is a hint that he, upon him be blessings and peace, is no innovation among the messengers, for guiding callers to God passed before him, peace be upon them.

Or the meaning is: for every people there is a guide of great standing, able to guide them, who is God, glorified is He. So your task is only to warn them, not to guide them, and granting them faith and turning them away from denial belongs to God alone, as in His saying: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them, but God guides whom He wills﴾ (al-Baqarah: 272).

Or the meaning is: "for every people there is a guide" is a leader who guides them to right conduct, namely the Book revealed to them, which calls, under the heading of guidance, to what is good for them. That is to say: the secret of sending messengers and its unique sign is only the call to guidance and the making clear of its paths, while warning is against being carried away toward the places of ruin. He has sent down to you the best of guidance, so guidance through it is a great sign and a supreme miracle. As for the proposed signs, their matter is in God's hands, and sending them down may not bring guidance! God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them﴾ (al-Isra': 59), and ﴿What will make you aware that when they come they will not believe?﴾ (al-An'am: 109), together with what persistence after them entails, namely seizure without respite: ﴿the way of God with those who passed away before, and you will not find any change in the way of God﴾ (al-Ahzab: 62).

Al-Shihab said: It is permissible to take (hadin, "guide") as conjoined to (mundhir, "warner"), with the complement placed before it for the sake of the rhyme (fasila), which indicates the generality of his mission and the comprehensiveness of his call. It may also be taken as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "and he is a guide," or "and you are a guide." On the first reading there is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

And His saying, Exalted is He:

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[ 8 ] ﴿Allah knows what every female carries, and what the wombs lose and what they gain. And everything with Him is in measure.﴾ [ 9 ] ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Exalted.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 9]

﴿Allah knows what every female carries﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*jumlah musta'nafah*), an answer to a question, namely: why were they not answered in their demand, so that their argument would be cut off and perhaps they would be guided? [The answer is] that He is the Commander, the Governor, the All-Knowing, the One whose power is absolute, who does what His far-reaching wisdom requires, not what their foolish opinions desire. This is on the basis that "the Guide" (*al-Hadi*) means "the one who calls to the truth."

If the intended meaning is Allah, glorified is He, then the sentence is an explanation of His saying "a guide" (*hadin*), or a confirmation and affirmation of that. So [it is] in *al-'Inayah*.

Al-Razi pointed out that the verse is either connected to what precedes it, indicating that He, exalted is He, has wide knowledge, and nothing escapes Him, that their demand is obstinacy and stubbornness, and that by displaying their demand they only increase in obstinacy; therefore they were not answered in it. Or it is connected to His saying ﴿and they ask you to hasten﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6], meaning: He, exalted is He, knows all that is known. So He sends down punishment only according to what He knows to contain a benefit.

Then the word *ma* in His saying ﴿ما تَحْمِلُ (ma tahmilu)﴾ is either a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*) or a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). That is: [what she] carried, or what she carries of offspring, in whatever state it is, whether male or female, complete or premature, beautiful or ugly, tall or short... and other states, present and expected.

﴿And what the wombs lose﴾ means: what they diminish of the pregnancy. ﴿And what they gain﴾ means: what they take in excess.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Among what the womb diminishes and increases is the number of offspring; for it may contain one, and it may contain two, three, or four. It is narrated that Shurayk was the fourth of four in his mother's womb. Also among it is the body of the child, for it may be complete or premature. Also among it is the duration of its gestation, for it may be less than nine months or more than that. Also among it is the blood, for it may decrease or increase.

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[10] ﴿It is all the same to Him whether any of you conceals speech or speaks openly, whether one hides by night or goes forth freely by day.﴾

﴿It is all the same to Him whether any of you conceals speech﴾, meaning within himself, ﴿or speaks openly﴾, meaning to others. ﴿Or whether one hides by night﴾, meaning seeks concealment in a hiding place by night in its darkness. ﴿Or goes forth freely by day﴾, meaning proceeds along his path (sarb), that is, his way, which everyone can see.

**Lata'if (a subtle point):**

It is said that *sawa'* (equal) means "equality" (istiwa'), and that this requires mention of two things. Here, if *sarib* (one who goes forth) is coordinated with a part of the relative clause or with the descriptive element, it would refer to one thing only.

This has been answered in two ways. **The first:** *sarib* is coordinated with *man huwa* (the one who is), not with *mustakhfin* (one who hides), as if it were said: "It is all the same to Him whether among you there is a person who hides and another who goes forth." **The second:** it is coordinated with *mustakhfin*, but *man* here carries the sense of the dual, as in the line of poetry:

﻿"Let us not be like the two who, O wolf, keep company"

as if it were said: "It is all the same to Him whether among you are two, one who hides and one who goes forth." On both views, *man* is a descriptive (*mawsufa*) and not a relative (*mawsula*) pronoun, so the first two are understood in this way, so that the whole is consistent.

There is another view: that the relative pronoun is omitted while its relative clause remains, and the meaning is: "and whoever hides by night, and whoever goes forth by day." The omission of a relative pronoun that is coordinated, while its clause remains, is common, especially since the relative pronoun has been repeated three times in the verse. An example is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9], where the original is: "nor what will be done with you." Otherwise the negative particle would be placed out of its proper position, because if the second clause were understood as falling within the relative clause of the first by means of the coordinating particle, the negation would have no place. The negation accompanies the first relative pronoun, not the clause, and an example of this is the saying of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

﻿"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah, and praises him and supports him, is equal!"

meaning: "and whoever praises him and supports him."

This last view was transmitted by al-Nasir in *al-Intisaf*, and it is very convincing. As for the others' weakening of it on the ground that it requires omitting both the relative pronoun and the beginning of the relative clause together, and that although they mention the permissibility of each of these, their combination is objectionable, this objection is itself objectionable. The style of the revelation (*al-tanzil*) is the proof, and to it one refers for judgment in every field and path. Rigid adherence to the rules and rejection of what contradicts them is a result of bigotry, obstinacy, and heedlessness of the position of the revelation as evidence!

And His saying, exalted is He:

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 13, Verse 11 (Part 1 of 2)

Discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[11] ﴿For him are successive angels before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah. Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah intends for a people an evil, there is no repelling it, and they have not besides Him any patron.﴾

﴿For him are successive angels﴾: that is, for whoever conceals his speech, or speaks aloud, or hides himself, or goes openly about (sarab), there are angels who follow one another regarding him (p-3653). ﴿before him and behind him﴾: that is, from all his sides, or [they guard] his deeds, what he has put forward and what he has left behind. ﴿guarding him by the command of Allah﴾: that is, they watch over what he utters of speech and what he does of action, good or bad, by His command and permission; or [it means] for the sake of His command to them to guard him. So "min" (from/for) is causal (ta'liliyyah), or it carries the meaning of the causal "ba'" (bi). The grammarians make no distinction between ʿillah (cause/reason) and sabab (cause/means), though the rationalists (ahl al-maʿqul) distinguish between them.

In the Sahih [of al-Bukhari]: "Angels follow one another among you, by night and by day, and they gather at the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. Then those who spent the night among you ascend to Him, and He asks them, although He knows best about them: 'How did you leave My servants?' They say: 'We came to them while they were praying, and we left them while they were praying.'"

And in another hadith: "Indeed, with you is one who does not leave you except at the time of relieving oneself and at the time of intercourse, so be shy before them and honour them."

The word al-muʿaqqibat is the plural of muʿaqqibah, from ʿaqqaba, an intensive form of ʿaqaba. The taf'il form is for emphasis and increase in the act of following up, so it denotes intensification of the verb or the agent, not transitivity, since its base form is already transitive by itself. The original meaning of al-ʿaqib is the back part of the foot (heel); then it was figuratively extended to the act occurring without interval or delay, as if one were treading in the heel of another. Al-Raghib said: "ʿaqabahu" means when one follows him, like "dabarahu" and "qafahu" (followed his back). It was also said that it is from iʿtaqaba (to succeed one another), with the taʾ assimilated into the qaf; but this was refuted, since the taʾ is not assimilated into the qaf within one word or two words. The morphologists (ahl al-tasrif, the specialists in morphology) have said that the qaf and the kaf are each assimilated into the other, and are not assimilated into anything else. The taʾ in muʿaqqibah, the singular of al-muʿaqqibat, is for intensification, not for feminine gender, since angels are not described by it, like nassabah (a great genealogist) and ʿallamah (a great scholar). Or it is an adjective of a group and a company.

﴿before him and behind him﴾ is a stationary adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqirr) as a description of ﴿successive angels﴾, or a loose adverbial phrase (zarf laghw) connected to it. The "min" is for the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah), or it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in the adverbial phrase that functions as the predicate. The sentence is complete at His words ﴿and behind him﴾. It is also permissible for it to be an adverbial phrase of ﴿guarding him﴾, meaning: successive angels guard him from before him and behind him, that is, they guard what he has put forward and left behind of deeds, as a metonymy for guarding all his deeds. It is also permissible for ﴿guarding him﴾ to be a description of ﴿successive angels﴾, or a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the adverbial phrase before it, meaning that the successive angels encompass all his sides.

Admonitions:

First: What we have put forward regarding the meaning of the verse is the most well-known. From Ibn ʿAbbas: it is the ruler who has a guard before him and behind him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, they guard him in his imagination and estimation from the command of Allah, that is, from His decrees and calamities; or it is said in mockery of him.

Al-Razi said: this opinion was preferred by Abu Muslim al-Isfahani. The meaning is that in the knowledge of Allah, the secret and the open are equal, and the one hidden in the darkness of night, and the one who goes openly relying on helpers and supporters, who are the kings and the princes. Whoever seeks refuge in the night, his affair will not escape Allah; and whoever travels by day with the successive guards, who are the bodyguards and helpers who protect him, his guard does not save him from Allah, exalted is He! The muʿaqqib is the helper, because when this one sees that one, then that one must see this one, so the insight of each one of them becomes a successor to the insight of the other. So these successive guards do not deliver [him] from the decree of Allah and His destiny! And they, even if they think that they deliver their master from the command of Allah and His judgment, they absolutely cannot do that! The purpose of this sentence is to rouse sultans, princes and the great to seek deliverance from hardships through the protection and safeguarding of Allah, and not to rely on helpers and supporters in repelling them. For this reason He, exalted is He, said afterward: ﴿And when Allah intends for a people an evil﴾, and so on.

(p-3655) Second: We have mentioned that the pronoun in ﴿For him are successive angels﴾ refers to "whoever conceals or speaks aloud...", etc. Some of them made it refer to Allah, and what follows it (refers to) "whoever". Al-Shihab said: this involves unnecessary disjunction of pronouns. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the last "whoever", and it was said: it refers to the Prophet, because that is known from the context.

Third: Al-Razi, regarding the meaning of the most well-known interpretation of the verse, pointed out the secret of the specialization of the guardian angels to the children of Adam. Its summary is: they call to good deeds and acts of obedience by means of the inner motives toward them that a person finds in himself; and when a person knows that the angels record his deeds for him, he is closer to avoiding sins, because whoever believes in the sublimity of the angels and the elevation of their ranks, when he attempts to commit a sin and believes they are witnessing it, shame before them restrains him from undertaking it, just as it restrains him when someone of stature among men is present. And when he knows that the angels are counting those deeds against him, that too is a deterrent from them. And when he knows that the angels are writing them down, the deterrence is more complete!

﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people﴾: that is, of wellbeing and blessing ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾: that is, of righteous deeds or their dispositions, which are the natural disposition (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created people, to their opposites. ﴿And when Allah intends for a people an evil﴾: that is, due to their bad choice and their deserving of that ﴿there is no repelling it﴾: that is, there is no reversal of His decree concerning them ﴿and they have not besides Him any patron﴾: that is, one who manages their affairs and repels from them the evil that Allah has intended for them, because of what their hands have put forward of changing what is in them. In this is an indication that the failure of His, exalted is He, willing is impossible. And it is a declaration that they, by what they engaged in of denying the resurrection, seeking hasty evil, and demanding a sign, have changed what is in themselves of the natural disposition, and deserved for that the descent of the wrath and punishment of Allah, exalted is He. This is what Abu al-Suʿud conveyed.

Admonition:

In this verse is severe warning and fearsome, decisive admonition, that when those who adhere to the religion and those who affiliate themselves with it deviate from its straight path, incline with their desires, and abandon holding fast to its etiquette and its upright sunnah, there befalls them what transports them to trials and afflictions, divides their word, weakens their strength, and empowers their enemy!

(p-3656) In a sacred hadith in Ibn Abi Hatim: "There is not a people or a household that is upon the obedience of Allah, then they turn from it to the disobedience of Allah, except that Allah changes from them what they love to what they hate."

And in Ibn Abi Shaybah: "There is not a town or a household that were upon what I dislike of their disobedience to Me, then they turned from it to what I love of My obedience, except that I turn for them from what they dislike of My punishment to what they love of My mercy."

Al-Qashani said: in the change of blessings into calamities there must be a deserving, clear or hidden.

And from some of the early generation (salaf): a mouse tore my shoe, and I do not know that except for a sin I committed, and were it not that Allah empowered it over me! And he quoted the line of the poet:

"Had I been of Mazin, my camels would not have been plundered."

I say: what is transmitted from some of the early generation is to be understood as the intensity of fear of Him, exalted is He. Otherwise, the verified position is the distinction between what befalls the individual and what befalls the people, as the verse indicates. The Imam, the Mufti of Egypt, has excellently discussed this in (Risalat al-Tawhid), in the section on the Islamic religion, where he said:

"Islam has removed from the intellect the cloud of illusion regarding what occurs of the events of the great cosmos (the world) and the small cosmos (the human being). It established that the great signs of Allah in the making of the world proceed according to the divine laws that Allah decreed in His eternal knowledge, which no incidental occurrence changes. Yet it is not permissible to neglect Allah's role in them; rather, one should revive His remembrance upon seeing them, for it has come on the tongue of the Prophet ﷺ: 'Indeed, the sun and the moon are two signs of the signs of Allah, they do not eclipse for the death of anyone or for his life; so when you see that, remember Allah.'" In it is the explicit statement that all the signs of the cosmos proceed by one system, in which nothing decides except the eternal providence according to the laws it has established. Then he lifted the veil on the condition of the human being regarding the blessings that individuals or nations enjoy, and the calamities with which they are afflicted; and he separated the two matters (individuals and nations) with a separation that leaves no room for confusing them.

As for the blessings with which Allah grants some individuals enjoyment in this life, and the calamities with which He afflicts someone in himself, many of them are like wealth and rank, strength and children, or poverty, lowliness, weakness and loss; and the one who acquires or brings them may not be what the person is upon in his conduct of uprightness or crookedness, obedience or disobedience. Often Allah has given respite to some of the tyrants and transgressors, or the wicked and the corrupt, and left them the enjoyment of worldly life, granting them time until what He has prepared for them of lasting punishment in the Hereafter overtakes them! And often Allah has tested His righteous servants, and praised them for submission to His judgment; they are those who, when a calamity strikes them, express their sincerity in submission with His words: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 156]! So there is no anger of Zayd, nor pleasure of ʿAmr, nor sincerity of inner intention, nor corruption of deed, of what has any part in these calamities or those particular blessings, except in what is connected to the deed by the connection of cause to effect according to the customary pattern, like the connection of poverty to extravagance, humiliation to cowardice, and the loss of authority to injustice; and like the connection of wealth to good management in most cases, and standing among people to striving for their interests in most cases, and what resembles that of what is explained in another science...!

As for the matter of nations, it is not like that; for the spirit that Allah placed in all His divine laws, of correcting thought, rectifying reflection, disciplining desires, limiting the aspirations of appetites, entering (p-3658) every matter through its door, seeking every desired thing through its causes, preserving trust, feeling brotherhood, cooperating in righteousness, counseling one another in good and evil, and other foundations of virtues, that spirit is the source of the life of nations and the dawn of their happiness in this world before the Hereafter: ﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145]. And Allah will not withdraw His blessing from it as long as this spirit remains in it. Allah increases blessings by its strength and diminishes them by its weakness; so when it departs from them, happiness goes after it and rest follows it to its place! Allah replaces the honour of a people with humiliation, their multitude with paucity, their comfort with misery, and their rest with toil, and empowers over them the wrongdoers or the just, and seizes them by them while they are heedless: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they commit wickedness therein, and the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction﴾ [al-Isra': 16]. We commanded them with the truth, and they departed from it to falsehood. Then groaning does not benefit them, weeping does not avail them, what remains of the forms of their deeds does not help them, their supplication is not answered, and there is no remover of what has descended upon them except that they turn to that noble spirit and seek its descent from the heaven of mercy, through the messengers of thought, remembrance, patience and gratitude: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves﴾ ﴿the way of Allah with those who passed before, and you will not find in the way of Allah any change﴾ [al-Ahzab: 62]. How magnificent is what al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib said in his prayer for rain: "O Allah! Indeed no affliction has descended except because of a sin, and it has not been lifted except through repentance...!"

In line with these customs, the early generations of this community proceeded. While the Muslim was raising his spirit with these lofty beliefs and disciplining himself with the noble deeds that follow from them, another would think that he could shake the earth with his supplication and split the sky with his weeping, while he was in fact enslaved to his desires, persisting in his excess, and his supposition about the truth did not avail him anything at all!

When God Most High had warned His servants of the sending down of what cannot be turned back, He followed it with a demonstration of the signs of His power, His dominion and His majesty. So He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[12] "It is He who shows you the lightning, [causing] fear and aspiration, and produces the heavy clouds." [13] "And the thunder exalts [Allah] with His praise, and [so do] the angels, out of fear of Him. And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, while they dispute concerning Allah, and He is severe in might."

"It is He who shows you the lightning, [causing] fear" — i.e., of the thunderbolts; "and aspiration" — i.e., of the rain, that it will give life to the vegetation; "and produces the heavy clouds" — i.e., laden with water.

"And the thunder exalts [Allah] with His praise" — i.e., those among the servants who hear it, who hope for rain, exalt [Allah] while glorifying Him with His praise; that is, they cry out, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Allah." This is either by way of an elided modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), or a metaphorical attribution (isnād majāzī) to the bearer and the cause. Or it may be that the thunder itself exalts, in the sense that its indication of His oneness and His bounty, which merits His praise, [is itself an exaltation]. In that case the attribution is literal, and the figurative element lies in the meaning of "exalting" and "praising." For its indication of His transcendence above association and incapacity is likened to the exaltation and the verbal declaration of His transcendence; and its indication of His grace and mercy is likened to the praise of one who praises for what it contains of indications of the attributes of perfection.

Al-Razi said: "Ra'd" is the name of this particular sound. Glorification, sanctification, and what is similar to them are nothing but the existence of an utterance that indicates the realization of transcendence and sanctification for Allah, glorified and exalted is He. Since the occurrence of this sound (p-3660) is a proof of the existence of One exalted above deficiency and contingency, that is in reality a glorification. This is the meaning of His Exalted saying: "And there is nothing but that it exalts [Allah] with His praise" [al-Isra': 44].

"And the angels, out of fear of Him" — i.e., and the angels exalt [Allah] out of fear of Allah Exalted, dread of Him, and reverence. "And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills" — i.e., He destroys with them whom He wills. His Exalted saying "while they dispute concerning Allah" refers to the disbelievers addressed in His saying "It is He who shows you the lightning." He has turned to the third person, as a notification of their being removed from the rank of direct address and as a turning away from them, and as an enumeration of their crimes before everyone who deserves to be addressed. It is as if it were said: He is the One who does such wondrous acts as showing the lightning, producing the heavy clouds, and sending the thunderbolts, which indicate the perfection of His knowledge and power, and which those among the believers who understand them comprehend; or [the thunder itself and the angels], and they act in accordance with what this requires of exaltation, praise, and fear of His majesty, Exalted is He. "And they" — i.e., the disbelievers whose blunders have been related, together with their humiliation, abasement, and insignificance — "dispute concerning His affair, Exalted is He, by denying resurrection and by hastening the punishment, mockingly, and by proposing signs." Thus the "wa" (and) is for conjoining the sentence to what precedes it, His Exalted saying "It is He who shows you," as Abu al-Su'ud has stated.

That is: He shows you what was mentioned of the dazzling signs indicating power and oneness, while you dispute concerning it. "Al-jidal" (disputation) is the most intense enmity, from "al-jadl" (with sukun), which is twisting a rope or the like, because it is strengthened by it and its force is intensified. "And He is severe in might" — i.e., while the state is that He is severe in plotting, scheming, and contriving against His enemies; He brings upon them destruction from where they do not expect. From "maḥalahu," when he schemed against him and exposed him to destruction; and from it [comes] "tamaḥḥala li-kadhā," when he exerted himself in employing a stratagem and strove for it.

Note:

It has been mentioned in natural science that thunderbolts are sparks that burst forth all at once from the agitations of the clouds and their collision with one another, so a strong vibration occurs in the air. As for thunder, it is the sound that results from that bursting forth and reaches us slowly according to the distance of the clouds carrying the thunderbolts from us. According to the extent of the clouds, our hearing of the thunder's sound lengthens. When lightning flashes from the cloud, the effects of the thunderbolt have been completed; so when a gentle interval passes between the flash of lightning and the hearing of the thunder, its harm has been averted. But if nothing passes between them, such that the person is near the place of the thunderbolt and hears the thunder simultaneously with seeing the lightning, it is possible that he may be struck by the thunderbolt as it passes. As for the cause of the thunderbolt's explosion, they said: it is known that the release of electricity occurs only through the union of the electricity of bodies with one another; so when the cloud approaches the earthly bodies, the cloud's electricity seeks to unite with the earth's electricity, and a sparks of electricity bursts between them, which is the lightning. And then it is said that the earthly bodies were struck. This is the summary of what they said.

Al-Razi attempted to reconcile what was related from some of the early generation, that the thunder is an angel, with what has been established in natural science, in a way that removes contradiction. He said: Know that the verifying among the philosophers mention that these celestial effects are only completed by spiritual, astral powers; so the cloud has a specific spirit from among the astral spirits that governs it; and likewise regarding the winds and the rest of the celestial effects. He said: This is exactly what we have transmitted, that the thunder is the name of an angel among the angels who glorifies Allah. So this which the exegetes stated in this expression is exactly what the verifying philosophers mentioned. How then does it befit the intelligent person to deny it?! End of quotation.
