For its indication of His transcendence above association and incapacity is likened to the exaltation and the verbal declaration of His transcendence; and its indication of His grace and mercy is likened to the praise of one who praises for what it contains of indications of the attributes of perfection.

Al-Razi said: "Ra'd" is the name of this particular sound. Glorification, sanctification, and what is similar to them are nothing but the existence of an utterance that indicates the realization of transcendence and sanctification for Allah, glorified and exalted is He. Since the occurrence of this sound (p-3660) is a proof of the existence of One exalted above deficiency and contingency, that is in reality a glorification. This is the meaning of His Exalted saying: "And there is nothing but that it exalts [Allah] with His praise" [al-Isra': 44].

"And the angels, out of fear of Him" — i.e., and the angels exalt [Allah] out of fear of Allah Exalted, dread of Him, and reverence. "And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills" — i.e., He destroys with them whom He wills. His Exalted saying "while they dispute concerning Allah" refers to the disbelievers addressed in His saying "It is He who shows you the lightning." He has turned to the third person, as a notification of their being removed from the rank of direct address and as a turning away from them, and as an enumeration of their crimes before everyone who deserves to be addressed. It is as if it were said: He is the One who does such wondrous acts as showing the lightning, producing the heavy clouds, and sending the thunderbolts, which indicate the perfection of His knowledge and power, and which those among the believers who understand them comprehend; or [the thunder itself and the angels], and they act in accordance with what this requires of exaltation, praise, and fear of His majesty, Exalted is He. "And they" — i.e., the disbelievers whose blunders have been related, together with their humiliation, abasement, and insignificance — "dispute concerning His affair, Exalted is He, by denying resurrection and by hastening the punishment, mockingly, and by proposing signs." Thus the "wa" (and) is for conjoining the sentence to what precedes it, His Exalted saying "It is He who shows you," as Abu al-Su'ud has stated.

That is: He shows you what was mentioned of the dazzling signs indicating power and oneness, while you dispute concerning it. "Al-jidal" (disputation) is the most intense enmity, from "al-jadl" (with sukun), which is twisting a rope or the like, because it is strengthened by it and its force is intensified. "And He is severe in might" — i.e., while the state is that He is severe in plotting, scheming, and contriving against His enemies; He brings upon them destruction from where they do not expect. From "maḥalahu," when he schemed against him and exposed him to destruction; and from it [comes] "tamaḥḥala li-kadhā," when he exerted himself in employing a stratagem and strove for it.

Note:

It has been mentioned in natural science that thunderbolts are sparks that burst forth all at once from the agitations of the clouds and their collision with one another, so a strong vibration occurs in the air. As for thunder, it is the sound that results from that bursting forth and reaches us slowly according to the distance of the clouds carrying the thunderbolts from us. According to the extent of the clouds, our hearing of the thunder's sound lengthens. When lightning flashes from the cloud, the effects of the thunderbolt have been completed; so when a gentle interval passes between the flash of lightning and the hearing of the thunder, its harm has been averted. But if nothing passes between them, such that the person is near the place of the thunderbolt and hears the thunder simultaneously with seeing the lightning, it is possible that he may be struck by the thunderbolt as it passes. As for the cause of the thunderbolt's explosion, they said: it is known that the release of electricity occurs only through the union of the electricity of bodies with one another; so when the cloud approaches the earthly bodies, the cloud's electricity seeks to unite with the earth's electricity, and a sparks of electricity bursts between them, which is the lightning. And then it is said that the earthly bodies were struck. This is the summary of what they said.

Al-Razi attempted to reconcile what was related from some of the early generation, that the thunder is an angel, with what has been established in natural science, in a way that removes contradiction. He said: Know that the verifying among the philosophers mention that these celestial effects are only completed by spiritual, astral powers; so the cloud has a specific spirit from among the astral spirits that governs it; and likewise regarding the winds and the rest of the celestial effects. He said: This is exactly what we have transmitted, that the thunder is the name of an angel among the angels who glorifies Allah. So this which the exegetes stated in this expression is exactly what the verifying philosophers mentioned. How then does it befit the intelligent person to deny it?! End of quotation.

And His Exalted saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 13, verse 14:

(p-3662) The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words:

[14] ﴿To Him is the true supplication. And those they invoke besides Him do not respond to them with anything, except as one who stretches out his hands toward water, that it may reach his mouth, but it will never reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is not but in error.﴾

﴿To Him is the true supplication﴾ That is, the true supplication (du'a') through worship, humble entreaty, and turning in repentance; and the turning of the face is fixed for Him, the Exalted, and not for other than Him. Because He is the One who answers the one in distress and removes evil, He is the one worthy to be worshipped alone with supplication and seeking refuge. Thus the idafa (annexation) of "supplication" to "the true" is from the annexation of the qualified noun to its attribute.

In it is an indication of its association with the truth, its being specific to Him, and its being far from any taint of falsehood, loss, and error, as one says: "the word of truth."

Then, the Exalted explained the example of those who worship idols and claim (efficacy), in their lack of benefit and usefulness, by His words: ﴿And those they invoke besides Him﴾ That is, the idols whom the polytheists invoke besides Him, the Exalted, ﴿do not respond to them with anything﴾ That is, with any of what they request, ﴿except as one who stretches out his hands toward water, that it may reach his mouth, but it will never reach it﴾ That is, except with a response like the response of one who stretches out his hands, i.e., like the response of water to one who extends his hands to it seeking that it reach his mouth. Water is inanimate; it does not perceive the outstretching of his hands, nor his thirst and need for it, so it cannot answer his call and reach his mouth. Likewise what they invoke is inanimate; it does not sense their supplication, cannot respond to them, and is not able to benefit them! The purpose is the categorical negation of response, by depicting that they are most in need of it to attain their aims; no one is more disappointed in his effort toward what he is compelled to, let alone mere need. The summary: He likened their deities, when they seek their sufficiency in what concerns them with the tongue of necessity, to lacking awareness, let alone capacity to respond, and their remaining in loss for that, to the condition of water before a thirsty man who stretches his hands toward it, calling to it by expression and gesture. So he is, for that reason, increasing in thirst and in severe loss! The comparison here is, in origin, a compound figurative comparison, brought out in the mode of mockery, in that it attributed to water a response, increasing them in ruin and in regret. The exception is detached from the most general category of the verbal noun, i.e., they respond with nothing of response. The pronoun in (huwa) refers to water, and (bali'ihi) refers to the mouth; it is also said the first refers to the one stretching and the second to the water. "Basṭ al-kaff" means spreading the fingers outstretched, as in the words of the poet:

"He has accustomed the spreading of the palm, so that if he wished to contract it, his fingertips would not obey him."

﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers﴾ That is, their worship and seeking refuge in their deities ﴿is not but in error﴾ That is, in a loss with no benefit in it, since their deities cannot respond to them.

And the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 13, verse 15:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[15] ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows [as well] in the mornings and the evenings.﴾

﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows [as well] in the mornings and the evenings.﴾ This is an informing about His greatness, exalted is He, and His sovereignty which has subdued everything: that all the created beings, from the inhabitants of the higher and lower realms, submit to His majesty, His will, and His disposal of them, whether willingly or unwillingly, unable to refuse Him. Likewise, their shadows submit to Him, exalted is He, in that they are characterized, by His will, by extension, contraction, recession and disappearance. (p-3664) His saying ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾ may be a time-adverb governing (prostrate), with the particle "bi" meaning "fi" (in), and what is intended by the two is continuity, since he mentions the like of it for emphasis. Or it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to (the shadows), and the meaning is as mentioned. Or it may be said that it is a specification, since the extension and contraction of the shadows are most evident at these two times. This is what most have followed regarding the meaning of (prostration), so it is a metaphor for the submission mentioned, or a general metonymy (majaz mursal) since it is used for its necessary meaning, because submission in general is necessary for prostration.

In (Tanwir al-Iqtibas): the prostration is interpreted as worship and devotion, and (willingly and unwillingly) is made a distribution (nashr) corresponding to the order of the wrapping (laff). He said: (willingly) refers to the people of heaven from among the angels, because their worship is without hardship, and (unwillingly) refers to the people of earth, because their worship is with hardship. Then he said: It is said (willingly) refers to the people of sincerity and (unwillingly) to the people of hypocrisy. Then he said: (and their shadows) means the shadows of those who prostrate to Allah as well, and they prostrate in the morning on their right sides, and in the evening on their left sides.

Abu al-Su'ud said: It has been said that what is intended is the literal prostration, for the disbelievers, in the state of necessity, which is what is meant by His saying (unwillingly), single out prostration to Him, glorified is He, for it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Ankabut: 65]. And it is not far-fetched that Allah, exalted is He, creates in the shadows understandings and intellects by which they prostrate to Allah, glorified is He, just as He created them for the mountains until they were occupied with glorification and there appeared in them the traces of manifestation, as Ibn al-Anbari said. It is also permissible that what is intended by their prostration is what is observed in them of the form of prostration, following their owners. You know well that restricting the prostration of the disbeliever, in the state of compulsion and distress, to Allah, glorified is He, is of no benefit, for their prostration to their idols in the state of ease undermines the restriction derived from the fronting of the prepositional phrase. Therefore the correct reading is to take prostration as submission, and because the realization of the submission of all in origination and annihilation to Him, exalted is He, is more fitting for the rebuke against taking protectors other than Him, while the realization of their prostration to Him, exalted is He, is established. The specification of the submission of the rational beings in mention, though the others are likewise, is because they are the principal part, and their submission is evidence of the submission of others. End.

(p-3665) This verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 83] and His saying: ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled?﴾ [al-Nahl: 48], and so on.

Note of caution:

This prostration is one of the obligatory prostrations of recitation (aza'im sujud al-tilawa), so it is recommended for the reciter and the listener to prostrate immediately after reciting or hearing this prostration. Thus [it is stated] in (al-Lubab).

The commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted:

[16] ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" Say: "Allah." Say: "Have you then taken, besides Him, protectors who have no power to benefit or harm themselves?" Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are the darknesses and the light equal? Or have they assigned to Allah partners who created as He creates, so that the creation seemed alike to them?" Say: "Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Subduer."﴾

﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?"﴾ That is, their Creator. ﴿Say: "Allah."﴾ This is a command to give the answer from his side (ﷺ), indicating that it is the only answer possible; thus he and the opponent are equal in affirming it. Or He commanded him to relate their acknowledgment, signifying that it is something they cannot avoid, as if it were said: relate their acknowledgment, and then rebuke them with what the proof necessarily entails. ﴿Say﴾, that is, as a binding and rebuking challenge: ﴿Have you then taken, besides Him, protectors?﴾ That is: after you have known Him to be the Lord of the heavens and the earth, do you worship other than Him? Have you made what should have been the cause of monotheism, namely your knowledge and acknowledgment, into the cause of association? This is the explanation of al-Zamakhshari.

﴿who have no power to benefit or harm themselves﴾ That is: they have no power to benefit themselves nor to repel harm from themselves, so how could they have power over it for others? Therefore their worship is pure futility and folly! ﴿Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are the darknesses and the light equal?"﴾ Having shown their misguidance and the corruption of their opinion regarding the proof mentioned, He explained that one who is ignorant of it is like the blind, and one who knows it is like the seeing; ignorance of its like is like darknesses, and knowledge of it is like light. Just as everyone necessarily knows that the blind is not equal to the seeing, and darkness is not equal to light, so everyone necessarily knows that one ignorant of this proof is not equal to one who knows it. ﴿Or have they assigned to Allah partners﴾ That is: rather, have they made...? The interrogative particle is for denial. His saying ﴿who created as He creates﴾ is a description of ﴿partners﴾, included in the denial. ﴿so that the creation seemed alike to them﴾ That is: the creation of Allah and their creation. The meaning: they did not take for Allah partners who create like Him, so that the creation would seem alike to them and they would say: "These created as Allah created, so they deserve worship as He deserves it." Rather, they took as partners helpless beings who have no power over what creation has power over, let alone what the Creator has power over.

Al-Nasir said: In His saying, ﴿who created as He creates﴾ within the context of denial, there is mockery of them, because no one other than Allah creates any creation at all, neither by way of likeness and equality with Allah, exalted above comparison, nor by way of inferiority and deficiency. It would have sufficed in denouncing them that the partners they took do not create at all; but the phrase ﴿as He creates﴾ contains a mockery that increases the denial in emphasis!

﴿Say: "Allah is the Creator of all things"﴾ That is: there is no creator other than Allah, and it is not right that He should have a partner in creation, so He cannot have a partner in worship! ﴿and He is the One﴾ That is: the one who is singular in lordship, ﴿the Subduer﴾, whom none can overcome, while all else is ordered and subdued!

Then Allah, the Exalted, struck two parables for the truth in its firmness and endurance, and for falsehood in its dissolution and perishing, by His saying:

The meaning of His words, the Exalted:

[17] ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their measure, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from what they heat in the fire, seeking an ornament or a utensil, there is a foam like it. Thus Allah strikes the parable of truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it passes away as scum, but what benefits people remains on the earth. Thus Allah sets forth the parables.﴾

﴿He sends down from the sky﴾, meaning from the clouds, ﴿water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and valleys flow according to their measure﴾, meaning in proportion to their capacity, whether small or large. Each takes according to its size: this large one contained much water, and that small one contained what suited it. ﴿The torrent carries a swelling foam﴾, meaning it bears and lifts up, from the force of its surging, high foam upon the surface of the water. ﴿And from what they heat in the fire﴾, meaning from gold, silver and copper and the like, which are smelted in the fire, ﴿seeking an ornament﴾, meaning seeking adornment, ﴿or a utensil﴾, such as vessels and tools of war and tillage, ﴿there is a foam like it﴾, meaning like the foam of the torrent, which is the dross that the bellows expel. ﴿Thus Allah strikes the parable of truth and falsehood﴾, meaning their like: when they come together, falsehood has neither stability nor permanence, just as foam does not endure with water, nor with gold and silver and the like of what is smelted in the fire, but rather it goes away and vanishes. Allah explained this by His words, ﴿As for the foam, it passes away as scum﴾, meaning cast out and thrown away, so it benefits no one. Rather it scatters and disintegrates, goes off to the sides of the valley, clings to the trees, and the winds scatter it. Likewise, the dross of what is heated from the minerals goes away and nothing of it returns, and only what benefits people remains, of the water and the ore, as He said: ﴿But what benefits people remains on the earth﴾, meaning it stays in the earth, benefiting from it. ﴿Thus Allah sets forth the parables﴾, meaning He makes clear the parables of truth and falsehood.

Notes:

First: We have stated that this verse is a parable which Allah struck for truth and its people, and for falsehood and its party, just as He struck the parables of the blind and the seeing, and of darkness and light. He likened truth and its people to the water that He sends down from the sky, so that the valleys of people flow with it, and they live by it and benefit from it in various ways. And likened them to the ore from which they benefit in fashioning ornaments and making various vessels and tools, and that this remains on the earth for a long time, visibly enduring: water settles in its pools, and part of it runs through the veins of the earth to springs, wells and boreholes. Likewise the ore remains for extended periods. He likened falsehood, in the swiftness of its vanishing, the imminence of its end, and its stripping away from benefit, to the foam of the torrent and the dross of the ore. For it, though it rises, lifts up and swells, ultimately vanishes. Likewise, false doubts and deceptive fabrications may grow strong and become great, but in the end they perish, vanish and disappear, while truth remains manifest, unmixed with any doubt. For nothing endures except what is beneficial, and whenever truth and falsehood have contended, truth has prevailed with its horn...!

Second: His words ﴿according to their measure﴾ (bi-qadarihā) are a qualifier of ﴿valleys﴾ (awdiyah), or are connected to ﴿flow﴾ (sālat) or ﴿sent down﴾ (anzal). The majority of readers read the dāl with a fatḥah, while Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ashhab, and Abū ʿAmr in one narration read it with a sukūn.

Third: His word ﴿ihtamala﴾ (carried) [al-Nisa': 112] means the same as ḥamala (carried), so the form with the added letters has the same meaning as the basic form, as it is said. It appears to me that its choice over the basic form is for an increase in its meaning and strength in its structure.

Fourth: Awdiyah is the plural of wādi, which is an opening between mountains, hills or dunes. Ascribing the flowing to it is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), as in "the river flowed."

al-Samin said: He made awdiyah indefinite and sayl definite because rain falls on the land in turns, so it flows in some valleys of the earth and not others. Sayl is made definite because it was understood from the verb before it, which is ﴿flowed﴾ (fasālat). Had it been mentioned, it would have been indefinite. When it is repeated, it is repeated with a definite form, like: "I saw a man, so I honoured the man." End of quote.

Its origin is from Abū Ḥayyān, where he said: He made sayl definite because he meant by it what was understood from the verb. What the verb contains of the verbal noun, though indefinite, when it is referred to explicitly, becomes definite, just as if it had been stated as indefinite. Likewise, it is pronominalised when referring to what the verb indicates of the verbal noun, as in: "Whoever lies, it is worse for him," meaning lying. Had it come here as a pronoun, it would have been permissible, referring to the verbal noun understood from ﴿flowed﴾. It was objected: how can it be meant by what was understood from the verb, which is an event, while the mentioned definite thing is a concrete entity, since what is meant by it is the flowing water? It was answered: it is by way of istikhdām (a device in which a word is used in one sense and a pronoun referring back to it is used in another sense).

Al-Shihab said: This is not correct, and there is no artifice in it, as some have said. For istikhdām is that a word is mentioned with one meaning and a pronoun referring back to it is used with another meaning, whether literal or figurative. This is not so, because the first (the verbal noun) is an event that occurred within the verb, while this is an apparent concrete noun that is characterised by that event, so how can istikhdām be imagined in it? Yes, what they mentioned is the usual case, not exclusive to what was mentioned, for the pronoun may be a demonstrative, and so may the apparent noun, as in the words of someone:

*Sister of the gazelle in lifting her head and turning back*

The truth is that it was made definite only because it is known and mentioned by His words ﴿awdiyah﴾, and it was not made plural because it is originally a verbal noun.

Fifth: His words ﴿And from what they heat in the fire﴾ are another clause coordinated with the first clause, to strike another parable. ﴿Foam﴾ (zabad) is the subject, and its predicate is placed before it. The ﴿min﴾ in ﴿mimmā﴾ indicates origin, meaning it arises from it. It was also permitted that it indicates partitive meaning, meaning it is a part of it, but Abū al-Suʿūd rejected this, saying it disrupts the parable. His words ﴿in the fire﴾ are an establishing qualifier, because what is heated is in the fire and adjacent to it. It was said that it is an emphasizing qualifier. Abū al-Suʿūd said: The mention of the fire implies exaggeration in the process of melting and the production of foam. Not mentioning its extraction from the earth is because that aspect does not enter into the parable, just as the aspect of sending water down from the sky does enter into it, as detailed earlier. Rather, mentioning it would disrupt it. The secret of using the relative pronoun in His words ﴿And from what they heat﴾ etc. is brevity, by gathering the types of ores, while showing grandeur by treating them with disdain, as though the noblest of jewels is base in His sight, when He expresses their smelting by kindling fire with them, which implies that they are like base firewood, and depicts them in their lowest state. This does not contradict its being struck as a parable of truth, because the station of grandeur requires treating it with disdain, while also indicating that it is desired and beneficial, through His words ﴿seeking an ornament or a utensil﴾. Thus each of the two stations is given its due.

Sixth: We have stated that His words ﴿Thus Allah strikes the parable of truth and falsehood﴾ have an omitted modifier, meaning ﴿He struck their parable﴾. The secret of the omission is to indicate the complete correspondence between the parable and that which is paralleled, as if the parable struck were the very truth and falsehood.

Seventh: He began with the foam in explanation, in His words ﴿As for the foam﴾, although it is mentioned later in the preceding speech. In division (taqsīm), one begins with the latter, as in His words: ﴿On the day when some faces will be white and some faces will be black; as for those whose faces are black﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 106], etc., and He observed the order in it. You may say the point in it is that the foam is the apparent thing seen first, while the rest remains and is later in existence because of its persistence. The verse is of the type of combination and division (jamʿ wa-taqsīm), as al-Ṭībī detailed. So it is in al-ʿInāya.

Eighth: His words ﴿Thus Allah sets forth the parables﴾ are a magnification of the status of this parable and an emphasis of His words ﴿Thus Allah strikes the parable of truth and falsehood﴾, either in consideration of this being founded on the first parable, or by making ﴿that﴾ a reference to both of them. So it is in Abū al-Suʿūd.

Ninth: The Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Kathīr pointed to the abundance of fire and water parables in the Revelation and the Sunnah. He said:

In the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, struck two parables for the hypocrites, one of fire and one of water, and that is His words: ﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], up to the verse. Then He said: ﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky, in which is darkness, thunder and lightning﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], up to the verse. Likewise, for the disbelievers in Sūrat al-Nūr He struck two parables. One of them is His words: ﴿And those who disbelieved, their deeds are like a mirage﴾ [al-Nūr: 39], up to the verse. The mirage occurs only in intense heat, and for this reason it is reported in the two Ṣaḥīḥs: "It will be said to the Jews on the Day of Resurrection: What do you desire? They will say: O our Lord! We are thirsty, so give us drink. It will be said: Will you not come forward? So they will come forward to the Fire, and behold, it is like a mirage, some of it crushing the rest." Then He, the Exalted, said in the other parable: ﴿Or like darkness in a deep sea﴾ [al-Nūr: 40], up to the verse. And in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, on the authority of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, may Allah be pleased with him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of the guidance and knowledge with which Allah sent me is like the rain that fell upon a land. Part of it was fertile and absorbed the water, producing abundant grass and vegetation. Other parts were hard and held the water, so Allah benefited people with it, and they drank, watered their animals, and cultivated. And another part of it was barren plains that hold no water and produce no grass. That is the likeness of one who gained understanding of the religion of Allah and was benefited by what Allah sent me with, so he learned and taught; and the likeness of one who did not raise his head to it and did not accept the guidance of Allah with which I was sent. That is the likeness of the water." And in the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, on the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: "My likeness and your likeness is like a man who kindled a fire, and when it lit up what was around him, the moths and these creatures that fall into the fire began to fall into it. He tried to hold them back, but they overpowered him and plunged into it. He said: That is my likeness and yours. I am taking hold of your waists to keep you from the Fire, come away from the Fire! But you overpower me and plunge into it..." And both of them (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) reported it also in the two Ṣaḥīḥs. This is a fire parable. End of quote.

When He, glorified is He, explained the state of each of truth and falsehood in terms of condition and outcome, He followed it with an explanation of the situation of the people of each of them in terms of their outcome, as encouragement and warning, by His words:

(p-3672) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[18] ﴿For those who respond to their Lord is the best (reward). And those who do not respond to Him—if they had everything on earth entirely, and the like of it along with it, they would ransom themselves with it. Those will have the evil of reckoning, and their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾

﴿For those who respond to their Lord is the best (reward)﴾ That is: for the believers who responded to their Lord by obeying Him and obeying His Messenger, is the best reward, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿For those who do good is the best (reward) and more﴾ [Yunus: 26]. So al-husna (the best) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar), the relative clause, is placed before it. ﴿And those who do not respond to Him﴾ and they are the disbelievers. ﴿If they had everything on earth entirely, and the like of it along with it, they would ransom themselves with it﴾ That is: with what is on earth and the like of it along with it of kinds of wealth, in order to free themselves from what they face. In this there is a depiction of the terror of what they will meet that no expression can encompass. For this reason the phrasing turned away from saying "and for those who do not respond, the evil (al-su'a)," as the contrast would require. ﴿Those will have the evil of reckoning﴾ That is: in the Hereafter, so they will be called to account for both the great and the trivial. ﴿And their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ That is: the abode. And in His saying ﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾ there is an indication that al-husna is interpreted as Paradise, since it is understood from its contrast with it.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[19] ﴿Is he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only those of understanding remember.﴾

﴿Is he who knows﴾ i.e., believes [in]. ﴿That what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ meaning the Qur'an, ﴿is the truth﴾ — ﴿like one who is blind﴾, i.e., like one who does not know that. However, the intention is to disparage his state, so he is described as "blind." ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾ — i.e., the minds freed from adherence to habit and from following delusion.

(p-3673) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[20] ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah and do not break the pledge.﴾

﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾ i.e., with regard to what He has charged them with. ﴿And do not break the pledge﴾ i.e., what they have bound themselves to and accepted, of faith in Allah and other covenants between them and the servants. This is a generalization after a specification, and it contains an emphasis on the continuity understood from the form of the present tense verb. This was related by Abu al-Su'ud.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[21] ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined, and fear their Lord and dread the evil of the reckoning.﴾

﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ That is: of their kinship ties (arḥām), their relatives, and their believing brothers, by doing good to them according to their ability, supporting them, defending them, showing compassion toward them, giving them sincere advice, and restraining harm from them. ﴿And fear their Lord﴾ That is: they act for Him, or they fear His threat, so they do not disobey Him in what He has commanded. ﴿And dread the evil of the reckoning﴾

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[22] ﴿And those who patiently seek the countenance of their Lord, establish prayer, spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good—those will have the good outcome of the [Final] Home.﴾

﴿And those who patiently seek the countenance of their Lord, establish prayer, spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good﴾ means: they repel with good speech the bad speech that the ignorant address to them, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 96], and so on; or they follow the evil deed with a good deed to erase it. ﴿Those will have the good outcome of the [Final] Home﴾ means: the outcome of the world, which is Paradise, because it is the return place of its people. Thus the definite article in "al-Dar" (the Home) is for prior reference (al-'ahd).

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 13, verses 23–24:**

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[23] ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter, and [with them] whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants. And the angels will enter upon them from every gate.﴾ [24] ﴿"Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final home."﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 23–24]

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence which they will enter, and whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants﴾: that is, whoever of these believed, affirmed God's oneness, and did righteous deeds.

﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final home."﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 24]

[25] ﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth – those will have the curse, and theirs will be the evil abode.﴾

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[26] ﴿Allah extends provision to whomever He wills and restricts it. They rejoice in the worldly life, but the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment.﴾

﴿Allah extends provision to whomever He wills and restricts it. They rejoice in the worldly life, but the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment.﴾ This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children [means] We hasten for them good things? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55-56] The indefinite form of (matā') (enjoyment) is for diminution, as in the verse: ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah, and you will not be wronged even by the thread of a date-seed."﴾ [al-Nisa': 77] And He said: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life,﴾ [al-A'la: 16] ﴿while the Hereafter is better and more enduring.﴾ [al-A'la: 17]

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 13, verse 27:

The discussion of the interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying:

[27] ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself those who turn back in repentance."﴾

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ like their saying: ﴿So let him bring us a sign, as the former messengers were sent [with signs]﴾ [al-Anbiya' 5]. The discussion of this has preceded more than once. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself those who turn back in repentance."﴾ is a sentence that functions as an expression of wonder at their saying, indicating that it belongs to the category of obstinacy and demanding what wisdom does not require of tangible signs, after whose coming no one is given respite, not to the category of seeking guidance. Otherwise, if their aim were seeking guidance through a sign, the sending down of this Book, with its like, upon him, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, would have sufficed them as a sign, for it is the sign of signs...! But they are a people (p-3676) who preferred misguidance over guidance; they turned away from it, so Allah turned their hearts away. So He omitted what this sentence indicates, for brevity, since it is already known.

Abu al-Su'ud said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills"﴾ His leaving astray is a will that follows wisdom, which calls for it; that is, He creates misguidance in him by turning his choice toward attaining it, and leaves him immersed in it, because He knows that kindness does not benefit him and guidance does not profit him, like one who has your characteristics in arrogance and obstinacy, and excess in corruption. There is no way for him to be guided, even if every sign came to him.

Then he said: ﴿and guides to Himself those who turn back in repentance﴾ that is: those who turn to the truth and reflect upon the manifold clear proofs that were sent down. The reality of repentance (inabah) is entering into the state of goodness. Mentioning it in the relative clause rather than mentioning the will is as in the first relative clause, for the purpose of drawing attention to what calls to guidance, and indeed to its will, and to indicating what prompted the first will: obstinacy. In it there is an urging for the disbelievers to desist from the arrogance and obstinacy they are upon. The use of the past tense form indicates that guidance is granted in response to a prior turning back, just as the use of the present tense form in the first relative clause indicates the continuation of the will in accordance with the continuation of their obstinacy. End.

And His saying, may He be exalted:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[28] ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God. Indeed, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest.﴾

﴿Those who believe﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "whoever turns back" (man anāb), meaning: they believe in God, His Messenger, and His Book. ﴿And whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God﴾ means their hearts are at peace and fear (takhshā) at the mention of Him, and are content (tarḍā) with Him as Protector (mawlā) and Helper (naṣīr). The shift to the present tense (muḍāriʿ) form serves to convey the continuity and persistence of this tranquility. ﴿Indeed, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾ means: only through His remembrance, and nothing else, do hearts find rest, being comforted by Him, relying upon Him, and hoping in Him. Some scholars supplied an omitted noun (muḍāf), meaning: through the remembrance of His mercy and His forgiveness, or through the remembrance of His signs that point to His oneness. Others held that the intended meaning of ﴿the remembrance of God﴾ is the Qur'an, because it is called a remembrance (dhikr), as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And this is a blessed remembrance which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 50], and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Remembrance, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 9]. This is because it is a clear sign that calms the hearts and firms up certainty within them. This meaning fits His saying: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27], meaning: these people deny that it is a sign, while the believers know that it is the greatest of signs, by which their hearts find rest through the coolness of certainty. Al-Shihāb said: this is the most fitting of the interpretations.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[29] ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds: ṭūbā (blessedness) is for them, and a good return.﴾

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) may be the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject) of the sentence, and ﴿ṭūbā lahum﴾ is a second subject and a predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate) in the position of the first predicate. Alternatively, it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are." It may also be a substitute (badal) for ﴿anāba﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27]. The sentence ﴿ṭūbā lahum﴾ is either supplicatory (du'a'iyyah) or declarative (khabariyyah).

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Ṭūbā" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from "ṭāba," like bushrā and zulfā. The meaning of "ṭūbā laka" is: you have attained good and goodness. Its place in the sentence is either accusative (naṣb) or nominative (raf'), like your saying: ṭayyiban laka, ṭayyibun laka, salāman laka and salāmun laka. The reading in His saying "wa-ḥusnu ma'āb" with both the nominative and the accusative shows you both of its positions. The lām in ﴿lahum﴾ is for clarification (lil-bayān), like it is in "suqyan laka." The wāw in "ṭūbā" has changed from a yā', because of the ḍammah before it. Thaʿlab said: it has been read as "ṭūbān lahum" with tanwīn.

Al-Fāsī said: Whoever puts tanwīn on "ṭūbā" makes it a verbal noun without an alif, like suqyā. Some people claimed that it is a non-Arabic word. In Lisān al-ʿArab, from Qatādah, it is said that it is an Arabic word; the Arabs say: "ṭūbā laka if you do such and such," and he recited:

*Blessed is the one who exchanges the mountain for villages,
and milk for the green gourds and wheat of Iraq.*

Risl: milk. Ṭawd: mountain. Fūm: bread and wheat. Thus is it in Tāj al-ʿArūs.

(p-3678) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[30] ﴿Thus We have sent you to a community before which other communities have passed away, so that you may recite to them that which We have revealed to you, while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say: "He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return."﴾

﴿Thus We have sent you to a community before which other communities have passed away﴾, i.e., gone by, ﴿so that you may recite to them that which We have revealed to you﴾, i.e., that you may convey to them this great revelation and this wise reminder, just as the messengers before you conveyed to their peoples. His words, ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, form a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah) or a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafah), meaning: they disbelieve in the One of Wide Mercy, whose mercy encompasses everything. The turning to this attribute, which indicates mercy, points to the fact that the sending (of the messenger) arises from it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ: 107]; and it points to the fact that they did not thank God for the blessing of this revelation, which is the basis of religious and worldly benefits; and to the fact that al-Raḥmān is among His beautiful names and sublime attributes, yet they used to shun this noble name. For this reason, on the day of al-Ḥudaybiyyah, they refused to let (the scribe) write "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," and said: "We do not know what al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm is," as is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ. And God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Say: "Call upon God or call upon the Most Merciful"﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 110]. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, on the authority of Ibn ʿUmar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The most beloved of names to God are ʿAbd Allāh and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān."

﴿Say: "He"﴾, i.e., al-Raḥmān, whom you disbelieved in and whose knowledge you denied: ﴿"is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return"﴾, i.e., my repentance and my turning back, for none other than Him deserves that. Then, exalted is He, pointed to the greatness of this revelation and its superiority over everything else by His saying:

[p. 3679]

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[31] ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which the mountains were set in motion, or by which the earth were split asunder, or by which the dead were made to speak, [it would be this Qur'an]. Rather, the command belongs entirely to God. Have not those who believe despaired that, if God willed, He would guide all the people? And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done, or it will settle near their dwelling, until the promise of God comes. Indeed God does not break His promise.﴾

﴿And if there were a Qur'an﴾, meaning any Qur'an at all, ﴿by which﴾, that is, by its being sent down or by its being recited, ﴿the mountains were set in motion﴾, that is, they were removed from their places and shaken from their positions, ﴿or by which the earth were split asunder﴾, that is, it were cleft until it cracked and became pieces, ﴿or by which the dead were made to speak﴾, that is, they were addressed after being brought to life by its recitation over them. The answer (jawab) is omitted, meaning: this Qur'an would have been (the one that does these things), because it is the utmost in guidance and admonition, and the ultimate in warning and intimidation. On this reading, the purpose is to show the great stature of the Qur'an and the corruption of the opinion of the disbelievers, in that they did not esteem it its lofty worth and did not count it among the signs, so they proposed other things, such as what was given to Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both.

Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) supposed the answer to be "(it would not have helped) when they believed in it," like His saying: ﴿And if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them﴾ [al-An'am: 111], and so on. On this view, the purpose is to show their extremity in obstinacy and arrogance and their persistence in error and corruption.

It is related from al-Farra' (d. 207 AH) that the answer is placed before it, namely His saying: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30], and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. But this is remote and forced. Some have pointed out that his intention is that the verse is the indication of the answer. The masculine form in (kallama) is due to giving precedence to the masculine among the dead over others.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, the command belongs entirely to God﴾, meaning: to Him belongs the command upon which the sphere of existence turns, in being and non-being. He does what He wills and decides what He desires, for the sake of the far-reaching wisdoms He intends. This is a turning away (idrab) from what the (particle) "law" (law) contains of the sense of negation, meaning: if a Qur'an had been made to do what was mentioned, it would have been this Qur'an, [p. 3680] but it was not so done. Rather, He did what is the case now, because the whole command belongs to Him alone. On the earlier reading of al-Zajjaj, the turning away is directed at what preceded of their proposals, together with their stubbornness as explained. That is: they have no such right, rather the command belongs entirely to God. If He wills, He brings what they propose, and if He wills, He does not bring it, according to what wisdom requires, without anyone having any power of dictating or proposing to Him. Thus in Abu al-Su'ud.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired that, if God willed, He would guide all the people?﴾, meaning: has not the one who believes known and become clear (that...). Like his saying:

*Have not the peoples despaired that I am his son, though I am far from the land of my kin?*

And his saying:

*I say to them at the mountain pass when they divide me up as a share: did you not know that I am the son of the horseman Zahdam?*

That is: did you not know! (The verb) yuyassirunani is from (al-yasar), the dividing of the slaughtered camel, that is, they apportion me. It is also reported as ya'sirunani, from (al-asr), captivity. The meaning: have they not known that He, exalted is He, if He willed their guidance, would have guided them, because the command is His. But wisdom required that the foundation of obligation be on choice.

﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease﴾, that is, from the people of Makkah, ﴿to be struck by a calamity for what they have done﴾, that is, because of what they did of disbelief and persistence in it, and their failure to explain it, whether by exaggerating it or by repudiating it. The *qari'ah* is the great affliction that strikes and shakes, meaning: the kinds of trials and disasters that would befall them, such as killing, captivity, plundering and despoiling, ﴿or it settles﴾, that is, that calamity settles, ﴿near﴾, that is, in a nearby place, ﴿their dwelling﴾, so that they are frightened by it and its sparks fly to them, ﴿until the promise of God comes﴾, that is, the conquest of Makkah, ﴿indeed God does not break His promise﴾, that is, He does not violate His promise to His messengers of victory for them and their followers in this world and the Hereafter, as He said: ﴿So do not think that God would break His promise to His messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 47].

There is another interpretation of the verse, which takes "those who disbelieve" to refer to all the disbelievers. That is: they will not cease, because of their denial, to be struck by calamities in this world, or calamities will strike those around them so that they may take warning, as He said: ﴿And We destroyed what was around you of the cities and We varied the signs so that they might return﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 27], and His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its edges? Are they the victors?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 44].

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 13, verse 32:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[32] ﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but I gave respite to those who disbelieved; then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾

﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but I gave respite to those who disbelieved﴾ That is: I granted them a respite and left them for a long period of time, in security and ease, as a beast is left to graze: ﴿then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾ That is: My punishment of them. In this there is an indication of its severity that is not hidden. The verse is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he encountered from the polytheists of denial and of making demands, in the manner of mockery directed at him, and a warning to them.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 13, verse 33:**

(p-3682) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[33] ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like those who have no such attribute]? Yet they ascribe partners to God. Say: "Name them. Or will you inform Him of something He does not know on the earth, or is it merely an outward saying?" Rather, the scheming of those who disbelieve has been made attractive to them, and they have been barred from the way. And whomever God leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾

﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾ means: watching over its states and witnessing them, nothing of what it earns of good or evil being hidden from Him. This is a majaz (figurative usage), because one who "stands over" a thing knows it. That is why it is said, "waqafa 'alayhi" (he came to know of it) when someone knows it and nothing of his conditions remains hidden from him. The predicate is omitted, its implied sense being: "like one who is not such." It is omitted because the context indicates it, namely His words, ﴿and they ascribe partners to God﴾, meaning they worshipped alongside Him idols, rivals and images.

His words ﴿Say: "Name them"﴾ are a rebuke following upon a rebuke. The meaning is: name them, who are they, and what are their names? For they have no reality! Or describe them, and consider whether they possess anything that would make them deserving of worship and qualify them for partnership.

Al-Razi said: this is said only of a matter that is so despised that it is not mentioned and no name is given to it. In that case one says, "Name it, if you wish," meaning that it is the lowest of things to be named or mentioned. But if you wish to give it a name, do so. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Name them as gods," in a tone of threat, the meaning being: whether you name them by this name or do not, they are so lowly that a rational person should not deign to turn to them.

﴿Or will you inform Him of something He does not know on the earth﴾ means: of partners whom He, glorified is He, does not know. If He does not know them, and He is knowing of everything that has been and will be, then they have no reality. This is a negation of them by way of negating a necessary consequence of them, through the device of kinaya (allusion).

Al-Nasir said: the reality of this negation is that they are not partners, and that God does not know them as such, because they are not such. Though they have fixed existences which God knows, these are created and dependent, not worshipped deities. But the coming of the negation in this manner, as recited, is wondrous, and its eloquence and mastery cannot be fully grasped. Had the speech come in its original form, not adorned with this wondrous variation, it would have been: "They ascribed partners to God, and they are not partners." It would not have had this placement that the recitation requires.

His words ﴿or is it merely an outward saying?﴾ mean: rather, do you name them partners with a mere outward saying, without any reality corresponding to it, like naming a black man "Kafur" (camphor) though there is no whiteness in him nor a pleasant fragrance, owing to extreme ignorance and feebleness of intellect? This is like His words, ﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], and ﴿You worship besides Him only names that you have named﴾ [Yusuf: 40]. It is also reported from al-Dahhak that the word "zahir" here means "false," as in the line:

*"And that is a shame, O son of Rayta, it is manifest."*

A note:

Al-Zamakhshari said: this argument, and its wondrous methods which occur in it, proclaims itself with a fluent and eloquent tongue: that it is not the speech of a human being to one who recognizes and is fair with himself.

Its commentators said: His words, ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul...﴾, being sufficient for demolishing the foundation of associationism together with what precedes and follows it, and what it contains of added subtle points, and being a refutation by way of truth, was appended with a refutation from the opposite extreme, in the sense: would that they, in ascribing partners, had ascribed them to one to whom partnership could not properly be ascribed, but they ascribed them to one about whom such a thing could be imagined at the slightest supposition. It was observed in this that the partners have no names and no reality, let alone a named referent, by way of an indicative allusion (kinaya ima'iyya). Then it was emphasized that they do not merit being asked about, by way of an allusive hint (kinaya talwihiyya), reasoning from the negation of knowledge to the negation of the known. Then from this it proceeds to the lack of merit, together with reproof, and to the supposition that they wish to inform the Knower of the secret and the hidden of what He does not know, which is an impossibility upon an impossibility. In the ascribing of partners, and in the disputing with the Messenger, peace be upon him, there is an informing of Him, exalted is He: a subtle point, indeed several hidden subtle points. Then He turned away from this. It was said: the sun has been made clear to one who has two eyes, and that naming is nothing but an outward saying with no substance beneath it, rather it is an empty sound.

Whoever reflects upon it with true reflection will acknowledge that it is the speech of the Creator of powers and capacities, before whose veils of secrets the understandings of humans stand still...!

His words, ﴿Rather, the scheming of those who disbelieve has been made attractive to them﴾, are a turning away from arguing against them. It is as if it were said: leave aside mention of what we were engaged in of the proofs of the corruption of their saying, because He has made their disbelief and scheming attractive to them, so they do not benefit from these proofs.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿and they have been barred from the way﴾ mean: barred from the way of God. It is also read with the sad vowelled with fatha, meaning: they barred people [from it]. ﴿And whomever God leaves astray﴾ means: He creates misguidance in him through his own bad choice, or forsakes him. ﴿For him there is no guide﴾ means: there is no one who could guide him.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[34] ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is harder, and they will have no protector from Allah.﴾

﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾: this is what befalls them at the hands of the believers, or the punishment within it of bewilderment (ḥayra) and misguidance (ḍalla). Indeed, the soul of the unbelievers is in constant distress and an incurable malady, for which there is no cure except faith, as He explained in another place. ﴿But the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾, i.e., harder than the punishment of this world in quantity and in quality. ﴿And they will have no protector from Allah﴾, i.e., no guardian who will shield them from His punishment.

(p-3685) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[35] ﴿The likeness of Paradise which the God-fearing have been promised: beneath it rivers flow; its food is everlasting, and so is its shade. That is the final outcome of those who have feared God, and the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire.﴾

﴿The likeness of Paradise which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, i.e., of those who guard themselves against disbelief and sins, ﴿beneath it rivers flow; its food is everlasting, and so is its shade. That is the final outcome of those who have feared God, and the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several aspects of grammatical analysis (i'rab):

(The first): That (mathal, "likeness") is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, i.e., "in what is recounted and recited to you is the description (sifah) of Paradise." The clause (tajri, "flow") is either an explanatory clause (mufassirah), or a resumptive clause (mustani'fah) of the explanatory-answer type (isti'naf bayani), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (wu'ida, "promised"), i.e., He promised it while determining the flowing of its rivers. This aspect is free of artificiality, together with what it contains of brevity, generality and detail. The predicate in it was assumed to be placed first because of the length of the subject's tail, or so that it would not separate the subject from what explains it, or from what is akin to an explanation of it.

(The second): That its predicate is (tajri, "flows") — following the pattern of your saying: "the description of Zayd is dark-complexioned" — it has been said: this is not sound in meaning, because it requires that the rivers are in the description of Paradise, whereas they are within it, not in its description; along with the feminine form of the pronoun referring back to (mathal) being taken according to its meaning.

(The third): That there is an omitted modified noun, i.e., "the likeness of Paradise is a Paradise in which rivers flow beneath it," and his saying (wa-zilluha, "and so is its shade") is a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "likewise."

(p-3686) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[36] ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture rejoice in what has been revealed to you, and among the factions are those who deny part of it. Say: "I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him. To Him I invite, and to Him is my return."﴾

﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture rejoice in what has been revealed to you﴾ because they attain through it meanings, proofs, and the removal of doubts that they did not attain from those earlier books. It was said: by them are meant the People of the Scripture (Ahl al-Kitab) who believed in the Prophet ﷺ, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, for they rejoice in what has been revealed of the Qur'an, because of the evidences they see in it for its truth, about which there is no doubt, and the manifest excellences and knowledge that cannot be counted. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture recite it with its true recitation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 121]. ﴿And among the factions﴾ means the rest of the People of the Scripture and the polytheists, ﴿are those who deny part of it﴾, which is what contradicts their belief. It is permissible that what is meant by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is those among them who rejoice in it merely because it confirms what came before it and honors it, even if they do not believe. By "the factions" are meant the polytheists, specifically those who deny what it contains of monotheism. Therefore He commanded that their denial be answered with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him. To Him I invite"﴾, meaning: not to other than Him. ﴿And to Him is my return﴾, meaning: my return for recompense, not to other than Him.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[37] ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have against Allah no protector and no defender.﴾

﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment﴾ That is: judging with the truth; or, an Arabic wisdom. ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have against Allah no protector and no defender﴾ That is: if you were to follow them in their religion, which is nothing but desires, after the knowledge has been established for you by the proofs and arguments, then no helper would aid you and no defender would shield you. This is by way of inciting, stirring up, and urging the listeners to steadfastness in the religion and firmness, and that no one who holds fast to the proof should slip when confronted with doubt. Otherwise, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was, owing to his great firmness of character, in a station far above that. Thus [says] al-Kashshaf.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[38] ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring. And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah. For every term there is a decree.﴾

﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring﴾ That is: like Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub and others. This is a rebuttal of their saying: "If he were a prophet, he would be of the kind of the angels," as they said: ﴿What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. It is also an informing that this is the custom of many of the messengers. So what was permissible regarding them, why would it not be permissible regarding him? Allah the Exalted has already said to him: ﴿Say: I am only a human like you, to whom it is revealed﴾ [al-Kahf: 110].

﴿And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾ That is: it was not proper for him, nor fitting, nor within his power, to bring what is demanded of him, except by the will of Allah the Exalted at its time. This is because the signs are fixed in correspondence with the times in which they occur, without change, alteration, advancement or delay. Their matter is dependent upon His, exalted is He, will, which is founded upon the wisdoms and benefits on which the affairs of creation revolve.

﴿For every term there is a decree﴾ That is: for every time among the times there is a written matter, determined, fixed, or obligated upon the creation at that time as wisdom requires. Thus the laws are determined by Allah according to the times; at every time that comes, a messenger comes from Him with what is the welfare of that time. And likewise all events, including the signs and others, so the matter is not according to the desire and proposals of the disbelievers, but according to what Allah the Exalted wills and chooses. In this there is a rebuttal of their haste for the appointed terms and for the coming of extraordinary events and punishment.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 13, verse 39:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[39] ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes (what He wills), and with Him is the Mother of the Book.﴾

﴿Allah effaces what He wills﴾ meaning: He abrogates (naskh) whatever of the laws He wills to abrogate, in accordance with what wisdom requires according to the time. ﴿And establishes﴾ meaning: in its place He puts what contains the benefit, or He leaves it as it is, not abrogated. ﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ meaning: its origin.

Al-Razi said: The Arabs call everything that serves as the origin of a thing a "mother" to it, such as "the mother of the head" for the brain, and "Umm al-Qura" for Makkah. Every city is a "mother" to the villages around it. Likewise, the Mother of the Book is that which is the origin of all the Books. Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: Allah changes what He wills, so He abrogates it, and establishes what He wills, so He does not change it. ﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ he said: all of that is with Him in the Mother of the Book, the abrogating and the abrogated, and what He changes and what He establishes. All of that is in a Book. And from Qatadah: that this verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106], and so on.

A note:

A group of scholars held to the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes﴾, and they said: it is general in everything, as the apparent wording requires. They said: Allah erases from sustenance and increases it, and likewise regarding the term of life, happiness and misery, faith and disbelief.

Al-Razi said: This is the view of Umar and Ibn Mas'ud. Those who held this view used to supplicate and humble themselves before Allah, exalted is He, that He make them among the happy and not among the wretched. End of quote.

(p-3689) He pointed by this to reports that Ibn Jarir recorded from Umar and Ibn Mas'ud. But there is nothing of them in the Sahih.

It became clear to me in Dammar on 12 Rabi' al-Awwal, in the year 1324:

Much of what many verses are cited for, in support of some objective, requires a more careful scrutiny of them, for the context of a verse may be for a matter that admits of no other, and one may suppose that he is citing it for another investigation. What may confirm this is what he sees of the consensus of many authors of works upon it. The matter rests only upon understanding the style, the context, and the preceding context.

Take as an example His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾. How often do you see someone citing it for the suspended knowledge and the erasure of what is in the Tablet, which they call (the Tablet of Erasure and Affirmation), and they bring up objections and answers that the one who stands over them does not find convincing or reassuring.

Yet if the reader reflects deeply on this verse, he would know that it has a meaning other than what they imagine. That is because they used to propose to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the beginning of the mission that he bring a sign like the sign of Musa and Isa, supposing that this was the utmost that indicates the prophethood of the Prophet in every time and place. So Allah, exalted is He, informed them that the role of those sensory signs had come to an end and its era had passed. Humanity has been prepared to be alerted to the rational sign, which is the sign of reflection and insight. Those signs were effaced just as their era was effaced. Allah, exalted is He, has established other things that are clearer, more manifest, and more indicative of the call, which is His saying before it: ﴿It was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah; for every term there is a Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38], ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾.

And His saying, exalted is He:

The commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[40] ﴿And whether We show you part of what We threaten them with, or We take you back [to Us] before that, your duty is only to convey [the message], and upon Us is the reckoning.﴾

﴿And whether We show you part of what We threaten them with﴾ — i.e., of the sending down of punishment during your lifetime; ﴿or We take you back [to Us] before that﴾ — i.e., before that occurs; ﴿your duty is only to convey [the message]﴾ — i.e., conveying the Revelation; ﴿and upon Us is the reckoning﴾ — i.e., their reckoning and their recompense.

Abu Hayyan said: The response (jawab) to the first conditional is (then that is your healer) and to the second is (then there is no blame upon you), and His words, ﴿your duty is only﴾ etc., are evidence for both of them.

And His words, may He be exalted:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[41] ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts? And Allah judges; there is no repeller of His judgment, and He is swift in reckoning.﴾

﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾ That is: the land of the disbelievers, reducing it against them by making the religion of Islam manifest in the outlying parts of their domains.

Ibn 'Abbas said: That is, do they not see that We open the land for the Messenger after land? Meaning, the diminishing of the circumstances of the disbelievers and the increasing of the strength of the Muslims is among the strongest signs that He, may He be exalted, fulfils His promise. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts? Are they the victors?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 44] and His saying: ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons﴾ [Fussilat: 53].

Al-Shihab said: This is connected to what precedes it. That is: He did not delay their punishment out of neglect, but until its appointed time. Or do you not see the loss of what is in their hands of lands and the increase of what belongs to the people of Islam? He did not address the Prophet ﷺ with it, out of glorification of him, and He addressed them to terrify and alert them against the slumber of heedlessness. The meaning of ﴿We come to the land﴾ is: Our command and Our punishment come upon it. End of quote.

It was also said: reducing it from its outlying parts means by the death of its people and the ruin of their abodes and lands. So how do these disbelievers feel safe from such events happening among them?

Note:

They mention here a report from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid that its reduction from its outlying parts is the death of its scholars, jurists and the people of goodness within it. What supports those who adopt this is that al-Jawhari related from Tha'lab that al-Atraf (the outlying parts) is applied to the nobles, the plural of tarf, which is the noble man. The witness for this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Ask about us and about you, when the people of Mina arrive, who follows the nobles of every tribe?"

He means the nobles of every tribe. So the meaning of the verse is: Do they not see what occurs in the world of changes: death after life, humiliation after honour, decline after perfection? And if this is observed and sensed, what secures them from Allah turning the matter upon them so that He humbles them after honour? It is not hidden from you that the early scholars did not mention this meaning as the tafsir of the verse, as its intended sense, but they mention it to magnify the gravity of the death of scholars, because they are the pillars of the earth, its righteousness, its perfection and its prosperity, so their death is a deficiency for it and a ruin from it. As Ahmad ibn Ghazal said:

"The land lives when its scholar lives; when a scholar dies from it, its outlying part dies.

Like the land, it lives when rain falls upon it, and if it withholds, destruction returns to its sides."

For this reason al-Azhari said, as in Lisan al-'Arab: The atraf of the land are its regions, singular tarf. And "reducing it from its outlying parts" means its regions, region by region. On this basis, whoever interprets "its reduction from its outlying parts" as the conquest of the lands is in agreement. As for whoever takes "its reduction from its outlying parts" as the death of its scholars, it is from other than this. He said: The tafsir is according to the first view.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah judges﴾ means: He judges as He wills. He has decreed for Islam might and ascendancy, and against disbelief humiliation and decline, as is observed from the signs and traces. In the shift from the first person to the third person, and in building the judgment upon the glorious Name, there is an indication of majesty, the cultivation of awe, and the confirmation of the content of the statement by pointing to the cause, which is not hidden. It is a parenthetical clause brought to affirm what precedes it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿there is no repeller of His judgment﴾ is a parenthetical clause within a parenthetical clause, to show the exaltedness of His judgment. It was also said that it is in the accusative of circumstance, as if it were said: And Allah judges, His judgment being binding, as you say: Zayd came, without a turban on his head, meaning bareheaded. The mu'aqqib is one who turns back upon a thing and nullifies it; its real meaning is one who follows it and pursues it with refutation and annulment. Abu al-Su'ud stated this.

﴿and He is swift in reckoning﴾ means: soon He will call them to account and requite them in the Hereafter, after the punishment of this world by killing and captivity.

(p-٣٦٩٣) The discourse on the interpretation (*ta'wil*, explanation of meaning) of His saying, exalted is He:

[ 42 ] ﴿And those before them had already plotted, but to Allah belongs all plotting. He knows what every soul earns, and the disbelievers will know to whom belongs the ultimate abode.﴾

﴿And those before them had already plotted﴾ means: the disbelievers who passed away plotted to inflict harm upon their prophets and the believers, just as these (disbelievers) have plotted. His saying ﴿but to Allah belongs all plotting﴾ indicates the weakness of their plotting and scheming, since it will be nullified and its effect will vanish, and that it is not something to be feared. The plotting that is truly to be feared is that by which they will be seized with varieties of punishment while they lie upon beds of respite, in a way that does not occur to them, as His saying, exalted is He, alludes: ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾, meaning, He will repay each soul the recompense prepared for it for the various kinds of disobedience it committed, among which is their plotting, from where they do not expect it. ﴿And the disbelievers will know to whom belongs the ultimate abode﴾, meaning, the good outcome, and upon whom the turning of fortune will fall. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they perceived not﴾ [an-Naml: 50]; ﴿So see how was the outcome of their plotting: We destroyed them and their people all together﴾ [an-Naml: 51]; ﴿So those are their houses, empty (in ruin) because of what they did wrong﴾ [an-Naml: 52], and so on.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[43] ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book."﴾

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you"﴾ For what is manifest of the decisive proofs and radiant clear evidences that testify to my prophethood needs no other witness. It was said: He made this a testimony (and testimony is a statement, whereas "sufficient" is a verb) by way of metaphor, because it suffices in place of testimony, indeed it is even stronger. End. It is not hidden that testimony is more general than speech and action. Moreover, the intended meaning of those proofs is the verses of the Qur'an and the Wise Reminder, which are His speech, exalted is He, and He has said: ﴿And they ask you, "Is it true?" Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it is true."﴾ [Yunus: 53]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ means: and whoever among the scholars of the People of the Book, for they find the description and attributes of the Prophet ﷺ in their Books, among the good tidings of the prophets concerning him. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿those whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157] and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 197]

It is narrated from Mujahid that by ﴿whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ he meant ʿAbdullah ibn Salam. This was challenged on the grounds that the surah is Meccan, whereas his conversion took place in Medina. Some answered that some Meccan surahs may contain Medinan material and vice versa, and as if this verse is of that kind.

Al-Hafiz Abu Nu'aym al-Isfahani narrated in (Dala'il al-Nubuwwa) that ʿAbdullah ibn Salam embraced Islam before the Hijra, when he travelled to Mecca before it and became certain of his prophethood, may the blessings of Allah be upon him. Then he returned to Medina and concealed his Islam until the Hijra took place. And Allah knows best.
